title: The War of the Worlds panic
hook: The great 1938 Martian radio panic was mostly a newspaper story.
peek: Orson Welles's 1938 radio play about a Martian landing is famous for causing mass panic across America. Historians now think very few people were fooled, and that newspapers, eager to make radio look dangerous, inflated the story.
lede: On the evening of 30 October 1938, Orson Welles and his Mercury Theatre on the Air broadcast a version of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds, told as a series of breaking news bulletins about Martians landing in New Jersey. The next morning newspapers reported mass panic. Later research suggests most of that panic never happened.

bullets.text: Front pages described terrified crowds and jammed roads, but the reports leaned on a handful of anecdotes gathered overnight. Newspapers were losing advertising to radio and had reason to paint the new medium as reckless.
A ratings survey that night found only about 2% of households polled were listening to Welles. Most radio listeners were tuned to a popular comedy show on another network.
A 1940 study by the psychologist Hadley Cantril estimated that about a million people were frightened. Later historians say his methods were shaky and his figure counted mild worry as fear.
The script placed the first landing at the small village of Grover's Mill. The village later embraced the story, and a monument there marks the broadcast's 50th anniversary.
